nameStory: Allen's Hummingbird is named after Charles Andrew Allen, a 19th-century California bird collector and taxidermist who first documented this western species. Allen was passionate about collecting specimens in Southern California, and this tiny jewel of a bird now carries his name across its western range.
description: Allen's Hummingbird is a small, energetic western hummingbird that very rarely strays into New England. Males flash brilliant orange-red throats and rusty-colored backs and sides, while females are more subdued with green backs and white bellies speckled with rust. Like all hummingbirds, they're tiny - about the size of a large moth - with needle-like bills and wings that beat so fast they create that characteristic humming sound.

idTips.label: Male throat color
idTips.description: Adult males display an iridescent orange-red throat patch (called a gorget) that can look fiery copper in sunlight or appear dark in shadows

idTips.label: Rusty flanks and back
idTips.description: Both sexes show varying amounts of warm rust or cinnamon coloring on their sides and back, more extensive than most other hummingbirds

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Compact and stocky for a hummingbird, with a relatively short, straight black bill and squared-off tail

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Males perform dramatic courtship dives with a distinctive sharp whistle or trill sound created by air rushing through their tail feathers

idTips.label: Female markings
idTips.description: Females have green backs with rusty wash on flanks and a white throat often dotted with small dark spots

habitat: In New England, Allen's Hummingbird would be an extraordinary vagrant, most likely found at backyard feeders or gardens with abundant flowers. Any sighting would probably occur during migration periods in coastal areas or urban/suburban settings where hummingbird feeders might attract a lost bird far from its normal western range.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to appear, but if present would be during peak migration when a bird might be most disoriented from its normal western route.
seasonality.summer: Virtually no chance of occurrence, as this species breeds exclusively in western states during summer months.
seasonality.fall: The most likely (though still incredibly rare) time for a vagrant to appear, when young birds might wander off course during their first migration.
seasonality.winter: No expected occurrence, as this species winters in Mexico and California, far from New England's harsh winters.

funFact: Allen's Hummingbird males are such fierce defenders of their territory that they've been observed attacking hawks, cats, and even humans who get too close to their favorite flowers, despite weighing less than a penny!
confusionNotes: In the unlikely event of seeing one in New England, it would most easily be confused with a Rufous Hummingbird, its western cousin. Male Allen's have a more orange (less red) throat and slightly different tail feather patterns, but these differences are subtle and require excellent viewing conditions to distinguish reliably.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, any Allen's Hummingbird sighting would be a major rarity that should be carefully documented and reported to local birding authorities. Most New England birders will never see this species locally, as it's a true western specialist.
compareHints: Allen's Hummingbird is nearly identical to the Rufous Hummingbird, with males showing slightly more orange tones in their throat patches versus the Rufous's more intense red-orange. Both species share the extensive rusty coloring that separates them from other Selasphorus hummingbirds like the smaller Calliope Hummingbird, which has distinctive streaky throat markings instead of a solid colored patch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relatives, the rufous hummingbird is the only Selasphorus species regularly recorded in New England, making identification easier.
Compared to its Selasphorus relatives like Rufous and Allen's Hummingbirds, the Calliope is much smaller and males have the unique streaky throat pattern instead of solid-colored gorgets.

Compared to its close relative the Rufous Hummingbird (another western species), male Broad-tailed Hummingbirds have rose-red rather than orange-red throats and lack the extensive rufous coloring on the back and sides.
